work.title: Homily for Holy Tuesday, on the council against the Lord

paragraphs.text: A sermon of John Chrysostom, Archbishop, for Great Tuesday, and on the gathering of a council against the Lord. And they said, “What shall we do?” The helmsmen of the church are like children who suck milk for their nourishment from their mother’s breast every day and constantly ask for it. And we too have become like a poor mother who has no milk because of hunger, but whose milk ducts have closed up. And just as someone might see a loving mother who has no milk, who sees her child crying and offers her breast, not to feed the infant, but to stop its crying, so you see us too. In just the same way you see us suffering the same thing and doing the same thing. For we too, seeing a new gathering, the children of the church standing around and waiting for the pure spiritual milk of the word, offer the breast of our mind, not to nourish them— for we are poor and destitute in words—but to quiet the burning of their love. But come, beloved,

let us hasten to the Gospel proclamation, to see the abuse that the Jews direct against the Lord. For it says, “The Jews gathered a council and said, ‘What shall we do?’” This is what John the Evangelist has told us today. For although he does not speak to us today with his mouth, nevertheless, through the Spirit he cries out into the ears of those standing here. For it says, “They gathered a council and said, ‘What shall we do?’” They assembled well, but the council was evil. Not for love, but for strife; not coming for peace, but arming themselves for war. They gathered a council, not to glorify God, but to dishonor Christ. They gathered a council, not to build up faith, but to overthrow the cornerstone. They gathered a council, not to bring the lost sheep into the fold, but to kill the shepherd and scatter the flock. They gathered a council, not to receive the pearl gleaming like snow, but to darken the radiant stone through unbelief, as they imagined they could. They gathered a council, not to gather a sweet cluster of grapes from the vineyard, but to nail the true vine to the wood of the cross, making it a vine of destruction for themselves, while preparing a vine of salvation for us. O council gathered by the devil against Christ! O council full of malice! O assembly of wolves nourished on blood rather than of God-bearing men! Why do I speak of savage wolves? They are worse even than savage lions. For the lions—Daniel

Although they had seen no sign, but had only seen the man and his goodness, they honored him and held their tongues. But the Jews, although they had seen so many such miracles, were driven by envy all the more toward murder. What did they say? “What shall we do?” Would that they had not assembled a council! Would that they had not spoken this way! Then their sinful malice would have come to an end. But they assembled a council and said, “What shall we do?” Oh, what a vile, carefully nurtured scheme! Oh, the groaning and sorrow caused by envy! Oh, the weeping and beating that serve no good! Not even Rachel, weeping for her children, groaned like this: “What shall we do?” When the poor ought to have rejoiced, when they ought to have been glad and made the day a glorious celebration, because the dead had risen, because life had appeared, because death had been destroyed, because the multitude of demons had been crucified, because humanity had been forgiven, because resurrection had been proclaimed to all the dead, now, instead of rejoicing over such great good, they weep and plot to destroy the one responsible for so much good. And they say, “What shall we do?” There was nothing else to answer except this: “Let us repent and turn back, fall down before him, and believe.” For what else would they have said if they had repented, except this: “What shall we do, since we have transgressed God’s covenant, since we have not kept the law given to us,

which says to us, ‘The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. Listen to him in everything he commands you’?” But now they do not say, “What shall we do?” out of repentance. Rather, “What shall we do? How shall we kill him? How shall we kill the righteous one?” O senseless Israel! [?] Have you not heard this either: “Do not kill the innocent and the guiltless”? Did not the blood of the former prophets pursue you— blood that cries out to God even now, awaiting vengeance from him? Yet even now, adding to that blood, you wish to shed the righteous one’s blood without cause, and you say, “What shall we do?” Oh, what a great mind without understanding, and counsel, and [?] flesh! A man who had been dead for four days came to life, and the bonds of sin were being torn apart, but they were deceitfully plotting to murder him, when they ought instead to have changed their words and said: “What shall we do, since we have reviled the Holy One, since we have not believed the Son of God? What shall we do? He swept away the lepers’ leprosy with a word as with a shovel, yet we did not believe him.” We saw those born blind receive their sight through him, and we did not believe him. What shall we do with him who fed five thousand with five loaves in the wilderness? Yet we did not believe him. What shall we do? He healed the flow of blood with the hem of his garment, and we did not believe him. What shall we do with the paralyzed man carried on a bed,

who had suffered this affliction for thirty-eight years, throughout his life? He healed him with a word. Yet we did not believe him. What shall we do? We saw him walking on the sea as though on land, and stilling the blasts of mighty winds and great disturbances with the breath of his hand [?], and we did not believe him. But they said, “What shall we do?”—not seeking repentance, but wrongdoing. Their field brought forth the dead alive without labor, like beautiful, ripe ears of grain. But they groaned. Or did you not reap what you sowed, O Jews? Or who among you received the Lord and suffered grief? Why do you weep, wasting away? For what do you wish to take revenge on God? Why do you prevent the dead from coming to life, driven by envy? Why do you wish to destroy the everlasting drops of the fountain flowing with honey, so that the thirsty may not drink? Why do you slaughter your oxen by wishing to kill their physician? But the cause of all this is evil envy. O envy, parent of murder, inventor of the devil, ruler of death! O envy, you do not allow those made envious by you to live, and you greatly torment those who harbor you! O envy, enemy of love, adversary of peace! O envy, courtier of demons, the devil’s trampling ground, dark flower! Those shepherded by you plot the murder of Jesus Christ.

From the beginning you envied Adam in [?], and when he had tasted sweet delights, you handed him over to bitter death. For there was no death in the world, but you, envy, gave birth to death. The word of Wisdom bears witness for me, saying that God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of life, but through the devil’s envy death entered the world. You stripped Cain the fratricide [?] of his white garments and sharpened the knife of wickedness for murder. You taught him to kill, and immediately made the wretched man tremble. You dwelt in Pharaoh’s heart and made the newborn Jewish children wither like grass. And however much good someone does you, O envy, why do you rise up all the more against your benefactor, like Saul, who was helped by David? And with your help, he became all the more inclined to envy. Jacob’s sons, having you with them, the beloved and wise Joseph sent into dark Egypt, and sold the free man as a slave. And their dream frightened us too. For the holy name showed [?] to be a figure of Christ. For eleven stars bowed down to him. Since Judas, who betrayed Christ, hanged himself, let us therefore flee envy, the parent of death, and rise and glorify God, who is above all, in Christ Jesus our God, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
